> The switch in sparse_8 could be simplified by dividing x by eight before the jump. Interestingly, gcc doesn't find this simplification.

It could not because that would ensure that 7 values for each case would be handled by function calls instead of the default case - 0/8 is 0, but 3/8 is also 0

What a shame for clang and gcc! They still don't implement perfect hashes for large sparse switch tables. I did that recently for my rcc C compiler, and it was just a single day of work. Esp. beneficial for unicode work. The LLVM patch was rejected a decade ago. Gcc has several unicode patches sitting in branches, which would also need that

I once played around with having a very large switch statement (all mac address manufactors in one switch) and in LLVM it would compile fine without optimizations, but if I turned optimizations on it would just spend around half an hour compiling it. I think GCC did it faster, but its been some time ago since I did it.  In the Rust crate that was the reasons for all this I just ended up doing perfect hashing which compiled much much faster.

> The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't)

Sometimes a decision tree is definitely faster. When developing System.HashCode, I used a switch (which I think always compiles to a jump table in .Net - at least my case did back then). This was for the trailing non-block sized bytes, I think. It was either suggested, or I decided to try, a decision tree and it was significantly faster. This was _many_ years back, so I don't have the figures, but they can be better in some scenarios.
Why the indirection? - why not have the jump table reference f0..fX directly rather than jumping to a jump?

I remember having implemented similar things in JavaScript (by generating code), for immutable Maps and Sets - no significant performance gain in modern engines. For regular expressions of complex unicode ranges, the speedup was around 2x!
I assume 34 in the compact_7() one was supposed to be 35, and edx was supposed to be used at some point in the bittest() one (unless i'm missing something lol)

In order to peak into hardware speculation/BTB, having a look atswitch lowering seems a good way. Big switches will go into serious convolution to please that hardware since by definition this is a source of a lot of branch mispredicitions.
This one was interesting, especially its name :)
